title: Open problem: ordered Ramsey number of matchings vs triangles
statement_text: What is the correct order of magnitude of $r_<(M, K_3)$ for an ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices? In particular, does there exist an $\varepsilon>0$ such that any ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices satisfies $r_<(M,K_3)=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$? (The authors can only prove the trivial upper bound $r_<(M, K_3) \leq r_<(K_n, K_3) = O\!\left(\frac{n^2}{\log n}\right)$, while some ordered matchings $M$ on $n$ vertices have $r_<(M, K_3) \geq c\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{4/3}$.)
context_text: An ordered graph on $n$ vertices is a graph with vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; an ordered graph on $[N]$ contains an ordered graph $H$ on $[n]$ if there is an increasing map $\phi:[n]\to[N]$ sending edges of $H$ to edges. The ordered Ramsey number $r_<(H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on $[N]$ contains a monochromatic ordered copy of $H$, and $r_<(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every such colouring contains a red ordered copy of $G$ or a blue ordered copy of $H$; for complete graphs the order is irrelevant, so $r_<(K_n,K_3)=r(K_n,K_3)$. An ordered matching is a perfect matching on $[n]$ with this vertex order. Logs are base $2$. The trivial upper bound comes from $r(K_n,K_3)=\Theta(n^2/\log n)$ (Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi and Kim). The authors prove that there is $c>0$ such that for all even $n$ some ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices has $r_<(M,K_3)\ge c(n/\log n)^{4/3}$, a considerable improvement on the trivial linear lower bound. They are not sure where the truth lies, but expect the upper bound to be far from optimal, and pose as a problem whether $r_<(M,K_3)=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ and all ordered matchings $M$.

title: Open problem: true ordered Ramsey number of matchings
statement_text: Close the gap between the upper and lower bounds for ordered Ramsey numbers of matchings: there is $c>0$ such that for every even $n$ some ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices has $r_<(M) \geq n^{c\log n/\log\log n}$, while every ordered matching $M$ on $n$ vertices has $r_<(M) \leq n^{\lceil \log n \rceil}$.
context_text: An ordered graph on $n$ vertices is a graph with vertex set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; an ordered graph on $[N]$ contains an ordered graph $H$ on $[n]$ if there is an increasing map $\phi:[n]\to[N]$ sending edges of $H$ to edges. The ordered Ramsey number $r_<(H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on $[N]$ contains a monochromatic ordered copy of $H$, and $r_<(G,H)$ is the smallest $N$ such that every such colouring contains a red ordered copy of $G$ or a blue ordered copy of $H$; for complete graphs the order is irrelevant, so $r_<(K_n,K_3)=r(K_n,K_3)$. An ordered matching is a perfect matching on $[n]$ with this vertex order. Logs are base $2$. The usual Ramsey number of a matching is linear, but the authors show that the ordered Ramsey number of a matching can be superpolynomial: the lower bound $n^{c\log n/\log\log n}$ holds for almost every ordering of a matching, and the simple upper bound $n^{\lceil\log n\rceil}$ (which in slightly weaker form also follows from work of Cibulka, Gao, Krčál, Valla and Valtr) almost matches it. More generally they prove $r_<(H)\le n^{cd\log n}$ for ordered graphs $H$ of degeneracy $d$. Related problems in the paper: for matchings of interval chromatic number $2$ (the vertex set splits into two intervals with all edges between them) one has $r_<(M)\le n^2$ and some have $r_<(M)=\Omega(n^2/(\log^2n\log\log n))$; for $q\ge3$ colours only $r_<(M;q)\le n^{(2\log n)^{q-1}}$ is known, and the authors ask for $n^{c_q\log n}$.
